--- author: Lukas Schmoigl title: Quarto Example bibliography: bibliography.bib --- # Example Repo https://github.com/schmoigl/test-project/ This Quarto file is showcasing what Quarto can do. Everything outside of code chunks is written in **Markdown**, a simple syntax for formatting plain text. ## Links Write links as `[text](url)`. Options go in curly braces afterwards, e.g. `{target="_blank"}` opens the link in a new tab: [This is a link](https://data-science.wifo.ac.at/lecture-notes/){target="_blank"} to the lecture notes. Since the output is a web page, you can also write plain HTML: Same link ## Text formatting One star makes text italic (`*italic*`), two stars make it bold (`**bold**`): *italic text* **bold text** ## Images Images work like links, but with a `!` in front: `![caption](path)`. Size and alignment are set in curly braces: ![Images](img/wu.svg){width=200 fig-align="left"} ## Formulas You can write LaTeX (TeX) formulas. Enclose them in `$...$` for a formula within the text, like $x_1 + x_2$, or in `$$...$$` for a centered formula on its own line: $$ x_1 + x_2 $$ ## Citations References are stored in `bibliography.bib` (linked in the header at the top of this file). Cite them with `@key`, and Quarto adds the reference list at the end of the page automatically: As seen @eppel2024active ## R code Code chunks start with ```` ```{r} ````. Options are set with `#|` at the top of a chunk, e.g. `#| echo: false` runs the code but hides it in the output: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ── ✔ dplyr 1.2.1 ✔ readr 2.2.0 ✔ forcats 1.0.1 ✔ stringr 1.6.0 ✔ ggplot2 4.0.3 ✔ tibble 3.3.1 ✔ lubridate 1.9.5 ✔ tidyr 1.3.2 ✔ purrr 1.2.2 ── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ── ✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter() ✖ dplyr::lag() masks stats::lag() ℹ Use the conflicted package () to force all conflicts to become errors Attaching package: 'kableExtra' The following object is masked from 'package:dplyr': group_rows Rows: 2518 Columns: 4 ── Column specification ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Delimiter: "," chr (2): case_nr, case_link dbl (1): case_address date (1): month ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data. ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message. ``` ::: ::: Without options, both the code and its output (here a table) are shown: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_data %>% filter(row_number() <= 15) %>% kable("html") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: With inline code (`` `{{r}} data$case_nr[1]` ``) results appear directly in the text, so numbers update automatically when the data changes: The first case is the case BG Telfs\, 6 S 12/06m ## Interactive elements (OJS) OJS chunks (```` ```{ojs} ````) run JavaScript in the reader's browser, so the page stays interactive without a server. Move the slider: ```{ojs} viewof rating = Inputs.range([1, 10], {value: 5, step: 1, label: "Rating"}) ``` I would rate this class `{ojs} rating` OJS can read the data that the R code saved above: ```{ojs} raw = FileAttachment("data/plot_data.csv") plot_data = raw.csv() plot_data new Set(plot_data.map(d => d.court)) ``` The chart and text below react to the inputs. OJS cells may appear in any order, since they update whenever a value they depend on changes: ```{ojs} import {vl} from "@vega/vega-lite-api" vl.markLine() .encode( vl.x() .fieldT("month") .axis({ grid: false }), vl.y() .fieldQ("cases"), ) .data(plot_data.filter(d => d.court == court)) // .config(config) .render({ renderer: "svg" }) ``` ```{ojs} viewof court = Inputs.select( ["BG Favoriten", "BG Fünfhaus"], {label: "Select a court: "} ) viewof month = Inputs.select( ["2008-01-01", "2009-01-01"], {label: "Select a year: "} ) numberOfCases = plot_data.filter(d => d.court == court && d.month == month).map(d => d.cases) ``` In the `{ojs} court` in the year `{ojs} month` the number of cases was `{ojs} numberOfCases`
